deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a physiological, not mathematical, page. It is a figure with legend, 'Fig. 7', for a note on the Vater–Pacini corpuscle (Vatersches Körperchen), the lamellated mechanoreceptor of the skin. The topic sits naturally beside Riemann's posthumous work on the mechanics of the ear and his contact with the Göttingen anatomist Henle. Henle and Kölliker published a monograph on these corpuscles in 1844.

The figure shows half of a longitudinal section. The straight vertical line on the left is the symmetry axis. Nested semi-elliptical curves meet it at the paired points a, b, c, d.
- aa: the outer boundary of the outermost capsule.
- bb: the boundary between the inner and outer capsule systems.
- cc: the innermost capsule, the sheath of the inner bulb (Innenkolben).
- dd: the length of the terminal nerve fibre (Terminalfaser) along the axis.

Shading encodes the assumed medium. The inner bulb is darkest, the inner capsule system intermediate, and the outer system lightest. Horizontal parallel lines labelled e come from the right. They represent the propagation directions of vibration waves (Erschütterungswellen) arriving from the outer skin surface.

Inside the corpuscle these lines are drawn bending at each elliptical interface, roughly along radial directions. They converge onto the axial segment dd.

The text states the claim conditionally. The waves are concentrated on dd 'if the darker-shaded parts have greater density and' — continued in the marginal note at the top right — 'lower elasticity than the sheaths' (falls die dunkler schattirten Partien größere Dichtigkeit und geringere Elasticität besitzen als die Hüllen).

Implicit physics (my reconstruction, not written on the page):
1. The elastic wave speed is c = sqrt(E/ρ), with E an elastic modulus and ρ the density. Greater ρ and smaller E both lower c.
2. So the inner layers form a medium of higher 'acoustic refractive index'. This is a layered, stepwise gradient-index convex lens.
3. By Snell's law, sin θ1 / sin θ2 = c1 / c2. A ray entering a slower layer bends toward the interface normal.
4. With convex, nested elliptical interfaces, the normals point inward toward the axis. Successive refractions therefore turn the incident parallel bundle e toward the axial segment dd, where the energy is concentrated.

Riemann's claim is this qualitative focusing ('acoustic lens') hypothesis for the receptor's function. No equations appear on the page.
errors: No mathematical errors are present, because there is no computation on the page.

Physically the focusing is only qualitative. Plane waves refracted at nested ellipses do not focus exactly onto a line segment; there would be aberration. In the drawing the rays are simply bent along roughly radial directions.

Acoustic wavelengths at physiological vibration frequencies (tens to hundreds of Hz) are far larger than the corpuscle, which is about 1 mm. The ray-optics picture is therefore physically inapplicable. Modern physiology sees the lamellar capsule as a mechanical high-pass filter, not a focusing lens. The hypothesis is historically interesting but not correct by modern standards.
The density and elasticity assumption is stated conditionally ('falls ...'), not justified. In reality the inner bulb and lamellae are mostly fluid-filled.

results.what: The concentric capsules of the Pacinian corpuscle, being denser and less elastic inward, act as a refracting (gradient-index) lens. They concentrate vibration waves from the skin onto the terminal nerve fibre along the axis.
results.modern_name: Acoustic or elastic refraction (Snell's law with c = sqrt(E/rho)); stepwise gradient-index lens focusing
results.usually_credited_to: Snell's law of refraction (Snell, Descartes) applied to elastic waves; the specific receptor hypothesis has no standard attribution

results.what: Schematic anatomy of the corpuscle: outer capsule, inner capsule system, inner bulb, terminal fibre.
results.modern_name: Lamellar structure of the Pacinian corpuscle

deep.surprise_reason: This is a qualitative physiological speculation applying elementary wave refraction to a sense organ. It fits Riemann's known interest in the mechanics of hearing and sensation and his Göttingen proximity to Henle. It is a mildly notable unpublished detail of his interests but contains no new mathematics or physics.

checkable.asserts: Wave speed decreases with density and increases with elasticity. So denser, less elastic inner parts have lower wave speed.
Snell's law: on entering a slower medium (c2<c1) the ray bends toward the normal, which gives the converging (lens) effect.
In water (c about 1500 m/s) at 250 Hz the wavelength (6 m) far exceeds the about 1 mm corpuscle, so ray-optics focusing is not physically applicable.

transcription_corrections: The marginal note 'Geringere Elasticität besitzen als die Hüllen.' is the continuation of the last line of the main text ('größere Dichtigkeit und ge-' + 'ringere Elasticität besitzen als die Hüllen'). It should be read as 'geringere', not as a separate sentence beginning with a capital G.
The machine transcription of the main text matches the image well. The insertion 'der Hälfte' replacing 'eines' and the struck 'bezeichnen' in line aa are correctly noted.
'86' is a later archival foliation in pencil, not part of Riemann's text.
